item.title: 7 Open-World Games With the Best Sense of Adventure
item.description:
Nailing the spirit of adventure is extremely important in the open-world genre. What’s the point of enormous maps and a story built around an epic journey if there are no surprises along the way? From stunning views and landmarks you can’t wait to reach and explore up close to well-hidden areas underground, high in the mountains, or deep underwater, open-world fans are always looking for that feeling of unexpected discovery in games they can play at their own pace.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

For this selection, I prioritize non-RPG, discovery-driven open-world action-adventure titles, focusing on worlds that sustain that sense of wonder . Even if some activities become repetitive later on, their worlds stay fresh through diverse regions that remain worth admiring and thoroughly exploring.

Crimson Desert

Immense Scale with Countless Possibilities

Ever since launch, Crimson Desert has been praised for its vast and beautiful world of Pywel, with players noting they haven’t felt this adventurous since Elden Ring or even Skyrim . Its scope is the first major draw, with some players spending 50 hours in the first region, Hernand, alone. Not that the other areas lack allure — even Hernand is packed with cities, settlements, enemy camps, deep caverns, gorgeous vistas, and smaller discoveries. Slowly learning the world’s rules, lore, history, and relationships between factions is a big part of its charm, but things only get more exciting from there.

New Open-World RPGs Basically Confirmed For 2027

From new entries in popular series to completely new IPs, 2027 looks promising for the open-world RPG genre, so what are we playing?

2
By Vlad Mazanko

Crimson Desert is in no rush to show all its cards, so you keep discovering things you wouldn’t expect to find even 50 or 100 hours in, be it intricate puzzles in the sky realm of the Abyss, steampunk architecture and robotic enemies in Delesyia, or the vastness of the titular desert itself. The game’s first expansion, Charting the Unknown, continues that trend, greatly expanding the map and adding full-fledged sailing and underwater exploration. There’s also enormous freedom you rarely find elsewhere. Almost anything you can think of is possible in Crimson Desert , even though some features serve no real purpose and are just there.

The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom

Synonymous with Unrestricted Adventures

Of course, no list of adventure games can do without Zelda , and while all eyes are on the Ocarina of Time remake, The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom is the current pinnacle of the series, expanding on Breath of the Wild’s winning formula of free-roaming adventure. Other titles quickly borrowed some of TOTK’s signature elements, with none other than Crimson Desert taking inspiration from its mesmerizing Sky Islands, a testament to Zelda’s masterpiece status and lasting influence on the genre.

Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Proves Fast Travel Has a Price

Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake nearly made Hyrule easier to traverse, but Nintendo decided the convenience came at too high a cost.

By Josh Cotts

In the realm of unrestricted adventures, Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom is up there with the best, even though it isn’t a full sandbox. Go almost anywhere from the start (provided you have the right tools or abilities) in this gorgeously designed world, use your creativity to build all kinds of things for traversal or combat, and tackle quests and puzzles as you see fit — there’s so much to see and do in TOTK that it can keep you occupied for months with satisfying, surprising adventures. Oh, did I mention there’s also an underground section just as big as the surface?

STALKER 2: Heart of Chornobyl

Learn the Zone’s Dangers Firsthand

A darker and much more dangerous adventure than most other entries, STALKER 2: Heart of Chornobyl still has a gorgeous world you want to explore despite its lethal nature. Literally every step in the Zone could be your last, but it’s still so interesting to venture deeper, encountering new dangers and untold riches. For the first time in the series, Heart of Chornobyl offers a fully seamless environment, as enormous and diverse as it is layered. Dangerous anomalies and mutants, roaming stalkers, multistory buildings, and underground labs keep delivering thrills (especially at night), while hidden stashes in the most creative places keep you guessing how to reach them and secure the valuable loot.

The Witcher & 5 Open-World RPGs Officially Returning In 2027

These open-world RPGs aren’t done yet, promising substantial reasons to revisit them or discover them for the first time.

By Vlad Mazanko

Hunting for legendary artifacts is especially rewarding in STALKER 2: Heart of Chornobyl , as each is tied to a unique anomaly or event with its own twist. Beyond that, your adventures are largely personal, shaped by random factors like artifact and enemy spawns, weather, time of day, your equipment, and your own goals. Most importantly, you won’t soon forget your first venture into the swamps, being caught by an emission at the worst possible moment, or finding a stash with a fine-tuned gun or suit of armor when you only meant to check a suspicious cellar or climb onto a roof.

Horizon Forbidden West

Uncover Mysteries of This Exotic World

Despite its obvious strengths, Horizon Forbidden West is largely absent from modern open-world discourse, and it’s not entirely clear why. The game is still among this generation’s most beautiful titles, while its tribal sci-fi aesthetics remain unmatched. More importantly, Forbidden West builds on the original in so many ways to deliver an even more refined adventure. The world is bigger, denser, and more stunning than ever, with more machine types to fight and weapons to find and upgrade, while new traversal tricks in Aloy’s arsenal make exploration much more flexible.

7 Open-World RPGs That Are Actually Worth Exploring From Corner to Corner

These open-world RPGs make getting lost feel worthwhile, rewarding curiosity with worlds that are far more fun to explore than simply cross.

3
By Josh Cotts

My personal issue is how the sequel saves its best parts, like flying and the world’s most vibrant regions, for much later, requiring hours of progression before you can experience the titular Forbidden West in all its glory. From there, it just keeps getting better: discoveries and lore revelations, exotic machine bosses, breathtaking underwater sections, and so much more. Sure, Horizon Forbidden West’s robotech direction might not be everyone’s cup of tea, yet it’s still among the most unique open worlds, blending fantasy and sci-fi to deliver a journey unlike anything else.

Subnautica

Stark Contrast to On-Land Adventures

Speaking of underwater exploration, it’s impossible to ignore Subnautica — an acclaimed survival adventure with a promising sequel still in early access. Its world is so different from the usual settings on land that the contrast alone is worth experiencing. Subnautica offers perhaps the most persistent sense of entering a truly new world, with surprises and discoveries piling up as you venture farther and deeper into uncharted waters. And by that I mean you’d better be prepared for how much stranger and more intimidating your journey can become.

5 Open-World RPGs That Make Skyrim's Exploration Feel Limited, Ranked

Some open-world RPGs take exploration far beyond familiar territory, offering unexpected challenges and remarkable discoveries.

By Nikol Nikolova

What makes Subnautica special is that discovery feels like a real expedition: you need to improve your equipment, plan how deep you can go, and decide whether that strange opening is worth the risk. A true free-roaming experience with plenty of replay value, Subnautica always has some unique hook you can’t resist. As mysterious as the oceans themselves, Subnautica is filled with memorable places that make you feel like a pioneer: kelp forests give way to enormous mushroom-filled caves, glowing reefs, skeletal remains, and volcanic depths. The rich fauna, with new creatures to spot every few minutes, adds another layer of discovery few other open-world adventures can sustain for long.

Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora

Forget Procedural Alien Worlds

Standing somewhere between Subnautica and Horizon Forbidden West , Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora takes you to another planet — one of fiction’s most convincing and well-thought-out places, where every alien plant, creature, and ecosystem has a purpose. Stepping onto Pandora, brought to life on such a stunning scale, can fuel your adventurous spirit as few other gaming worlds can, while its varied biomes and rich verticality make you feel like you’re traveling through an actual alien ecosystem, not just visiting differently colored, luminescent regions.

7 Open-World RPGs With Virtually Perfect Worlds

Open-world RPGs need to nail their worlds if they want to keep players engaged for the long run, and these massive games do just that.

3
By Amina Ayoud

In Frontiers of Pandora , you can visit entire biomes never properly introduced in James Cameron’s movies, including the sweeping Upper Plains and misty Clouded Forest, each with its own wildlife, plants, and Na’vi clans with distinct lifestyles. Like Forbidden West and Crimson Desert , though, Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora may take a while to reach its best parts, like getting an ikran to explore from the air. That changes the whole feeling of exploration: places that initially feel immense and difficult to cross become part of a much wider journey. Given that it’s a Ubisoft game, some repetition in activities and action inevitably kicks in, while the rewards for reaching Pandora’s most distant corners could be more exciting.

Ghost of Yotei

An Ode to Vibrance

Sucker Punch’s open-world samurai series instantly stands out with its art direction, depicting worlds so gorgeous and colorful they look better than real life. Ghost of Yotei can charm you from its opening moments: stunning scenery as far as the eye can see, the enormous Yotei mountain on the horizon (which you can climb!), authentic settlements, and countless smaller points of interest take you on a sprawling journey as you follow the wind. Every step feels rewarding, while the region-based structure lets the team portray vastly different areas, each with its own mood and atmosphere.

Biggest Open-World Games Releasing in November 2026, Ranked

Even if you don’t care for GTA 6, November still has something in store for open-world fans.

1
By Vlad Mazanko

Unlike Ghost of Tsushima , with its oppressive, war-torn mood and story-driven urgency, Ghost of Yotei is deliberately slower-paced, and playing as a sort of outlaw on a personal revenge journey has its own benefits. As such, every detour and small discovery can leave you better equipped for the major challenges ahead. Ghost of Yotei’s itemization makes exploration even more valuable: every new armor set or charm can drastically reshape your playstyle, while outfits and sword kits look exceptionally cool. Combining its visual allure, distinct corners of the world, and consistently valuable rewards, Ghost of Yotei plays like a true samurai dream.

item.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake - Dodongo's Cavern Walkthrough
item.description:
Dodongo Cavern is the essential dungeon you need to complete the Spiritual Stone of Fire in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (Remake). If you want to know how to access Dodongo Cavern, or you want a full walkthrough to ensure an easy completion of every puzzle and every collectible, then check out the full guide below.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
Zelda: Ocarina of Time - How to Get the Goron Bracelet

Goron's Bracelet is needed if you want to pick up Bomb Flowers. Here's how you can get this key item in the Ocarina of Time remake.

By Jake Fillery

How to Enter Dodongo Cavern in Zelda Ocarina of Time (Remake)

First, you're going to need the Goron Bracelet from Darunia in Gorn City, which you can get by playing Saria's Song in front of him:

Choose a song

Click here for a guide on how to get Saria's Song if you haven't obtained it yet.

After playing the song and getting the Goron Bracelet, head outside of Goron City back to the Death Mountain Trial, where you can head south to find a Goron standing by a Bomb Flower. Simply pick it up and throw it off the cliff, and it will land at the blocked-off entrance to Dodongo Cavern.

Before we proceed, you might be interested in seeing a 100% map of 1F and 2F for Dodongo Cavern!

Dodongo Cavern 100% Walkthrough (Zelda Ocarina of Time Remake)

Dungeon Map

Head to the center of Dodongo Cavern via the rising platforms and head west. There's a Bomb Flower to pick up, which can be thrown at the rock wall on the northwest side to find a treasure chest containing the Dungeon Map.

Gold Skulltula #1

Head east of the main chamber and use the Bomb Flower on the rock wall in the southeast corner to reveal a cave. Once you're inside, you'll encounter Baby Dodongos, but don't defeat them all! Lead one to the south wall and defeat the Baby Dodongos to blow it up and reveal a Gold Skulltula.

Puzzle #1 (Pressure Plate & Statues)

In the next room, you will find two statues. You just need to grab one of them and move it onto the pressure plate so that the gate stays open. You can then enter the next room to find two Lizalfos that you must defeat, which provides you with a chest containing a Red Rupee.

Puzzle #2 (Dodongos & Torches)

The next room has adult Dodongos, which can be defeated by getting behind them and attacking their tails. Once they have been defeated, use a Deku Stick on the lit brazier and light the other 3 unlit braziers to unlock the door to the next room.

Compass

There is a pressure plate to stand on in this room that will open the door in 1F to the west, near where you originally picked up the Dungeon Map.

Inside, look south and use a Bomb Flower to blow up the wall, which reveals 3 Armos statues. You can destroy the active one with another Bomb Flower! Now, take the ladder that was initially blocked by the Armos to open the treasure chest to get yourself a Compass.

Puzzle #3 (Bomb Flowers)

In the main room, there is a square structure covered in Bomb Flowers. To open the path, look to your right and pick up the lone Bomb Flower, then press A to drop it into the gap between the two Bomb Flowers. All the bombs will explode in a domino effect and drop the staircase.

Ignore the ladder leading to a rock wall, as you can't open it just yet. It only has a Business Scrub Seed, so it's not worth it.

Gold Skulltula #2

Head up the stairs and continue on the main path, but before entering the room, turn around to find a Gold Skulltula on the netting above, which can be shot with the Slingshot.

Puzzle #4 (Armos Statues & Boxes)

In the next room, there will be four Armos statues blocking the ladders. Ignore them, and instead head to the south. The Armos in the south can be pulled out to reveal the non-broken ladder, so climb it and step on the pressure plate to proceed.

The next room has a box in the right corner that can be pulled to the ladder. Climb up it and jump to the platform opposite to find a Bomb Flower, which can be thrown at the wall to let you through.

Puzzle #5 (Flaming Paths)

Inside, you'll find a burning platform. To deactivate the fire, look up and shoot the glowing eye with your Slingshot. You can continue on the path to find a room with Lizalfos, and when defeated, the next door will open.

The next room has two burning platforms. To deactivate the first, look up and shoot the eye with the Slingshot, then look left from the first platform to find the final eye in a wall. You can now proceed!

Bomb Bag

Continue west, and you will find a treasure chest containing the Bomb Bag. This will give you 20 Bombs that will be essential for the rest of the dungeon. For now, keep on the path and step on the pressure plate to allow the elevator from 1F to rise to 2F.

Gold Skulltula #3

From the pressure plate, head right and use the Bomb to blow up the rock wall. There are two Dodongos inside, but you can just head to the back of the middle rock and destroy the Gold Skulltula.

Puzzle #6 (Colossal Dodongo Skull)

Stand on the bridge on the west side over the Colossal Dodongo. Look at the gaps in the bridge and press A to drop a bomb on the eyes. When both eyes are destroyed, the mouth of the skull will open to reveal the path.

Gold Skulltula #4

Enter the skull and head northwest to find a rock wall. You can jump and throw the Bomb at the right time to explode it; inside, you will find yet another Gold Skulltula.

Puzzle #6 (Stone Cubes)

For this puzzle, you just need to move the first stone cube to give you enough height to reach the second on the raised wooden platform. You can then push this stone cube down to the next floor, and it can then be pushed south to climb out.

With the remaining stone cube, pull it out of its spot and then push it into the hole on the east side of the room. This will open the boss room as soon as you use a Bomb to blow up the rocky floor!

How to Beat King Dodongo in Zelda Ocarina of Time Remake

King Dodongo can be defeated by throwing Bombs towards his mouth as soon as he starts to suck in air . As soon as the bomb is in his mouth, he will be stunned, and you can attack his tongue. Repeat this until he dies, which will reward you with a Heart Container and the Goron Ruby when you leave the dungeon!

Head up the stairs and continue on the main path, but before entering the room, turn around to find a Gold Skulltula on the netting above, which can be shot with the Slingshot.

Puzzle #4 (Armos Statues & Boxes)

In the next room, there will be four Armos statues blocking the ladders. Ignore them, and instead head to the south. The Armos in the south can be pulled out to reveal the non-broken ladder, so climb it and step on the pressure plate to proceed.

The next room has a box in the right corner that can be pulled to the ladder. Climb up it and jump to the platform opposite to find a Bomb Flower, which can be thrown at the wall to let you through.

Puzzle #5 (Flaming Paths)

Inside, you'll find a burning platform. To deactivate the fire, look up and shoot the glowing eye with your Slingshot. You can continue on the path to find a room with Lizalfos, and when defeated, the next door will open.

The next room has two burning platforms. To deactivate the first, look up and shoot the eye with the Slingshot, then look left from the first platform to find the final eye in a wall. You can now proceed!

Bomb Bag

Continue west, and you will find a treasure chest containing the Bomb Bag. This will give you 20 Bombs that will be essential for the rest of the dungeon. For now, keep on the path and step on the pressure plate to allow the elevator from 1F to rise to 2F.

Gold Skulltula #3

From the pressure plate, head right and use the Bomb to blow up the rock wall. There are two Dodongos inside, but you can just head to the back of the middle rock and destroy the Gold Skulltula.

Puzzle #6 (Colossal Dodongo Skull)

Stand on the bridge on the west side over the Colossal Dodongo. Look at the gaps in the bridge and press A to drop a bomb on the eyes. When both eyes are destroyed, the mouth of the skull will open to reveal the path.

Gold Skulltula #4

Enter the skull and head northwest to find a rock wall. You can jump and throw the Bomb at the right time to explode it; inside, you will find yet another Gold Skulltula.

Puzzle #6 (Stone Cubes)

For this puzzle, you just need to move the first stone cube to give you enough height to reach the second on the raised wooden platform. You can then push this stone cube down to the next floor, and it can then be pushed south to climb out.

With the remaining stone cube, pull it out of its spot and then push it into the hole on the east side of the room. This will open the boss room as soon as you use a Bomb to blow up the rocky floor!

How to Beat King Dodongo in Zelda Ocarina of Time Remake

King Dodongo can be defeated by throwing Bombs towards his mouth as soon as he starts to suck in air . As soon as the bomb is in his mouth, he will be stunned, and you can attack his tongue. Repeat this until he dies, which will reward you with a Heart Container and the Goron Ruby when you leave the dungeon!

item.title: Bloodborne's Huge 2026 Sales Come With a Catch for The Duskbloods
item.description:
The Duskbloods is one of the most peculiar Switch 2 exclusives that Nintendo has waiting in the pipeline. The project marks the first time since the early 2000s that FromSoftware has made a game exclusively for a Nintendo console. FromSoftware games have built an incredibly strong reputation, and locking The Duskbloods with Nintendo's ecosystem is a bold move from both parties.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

After releasing games like Elden Ring and Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice , I and many others didn't exactly expect FromSoftware's next project to be a Nintendo0only affair. That alone is shocking enough, but the developer threw another curveball at gamers when the studio confirmed that the project is focused on multiplayer. Elden Ring Nightreign is proof that FromSoftware can do multiplayer, but it still isn't the developer's expertise. Nintendo risks a lot with The Duskbloods , and an unlikely source could be getting the company's hopes too high: PlayStation.

The Nintendo Switch 2 May Pay a Heavy Toll if Duskbloods Doesn't Deliver

FromSoftware's upcoming PvPvE game The Duskbloods is an enticing concept, but its sole platform may suffer if the final game can't deliver.

By Liam Ferguson

Bloodborne Is Still Drawing Strong Sales for PlayStation, Which Could Give Nintendo Misguided Expectations

What titles are considered the best FromSoftware games are going to vary from person to person, but a lot of the developer's fans see Bloodborne as one of the studio's greatest achievements. A recent report from Rhys Elliott at Alinea Analytics revealed that Bloodborne has still managed to sell an estimated 250,000 in just this year alone. That's wildly impressive for a game that turned 11 years old in 2026, and it speaks to just how beloved Bloodborne really is. There aren't many games that get to experience those kinds of sales and pop culture relevance over a decade after its debut. As great as that is, it could also be giving Nintendo the wrong idea about what to expect from The Duskbloods ' long-term performance.

One of the main details about The Duskbloods that got many excited when it was first announced was that it had similar vibes to Bloodborne . FromSoftware's multiplayer Nintendo project oozes the same gothic horror aesthetics that helped make Bloodborne such an unforgettable experience. With there being such strong hopes that a Bloodborne sequel will eventually be brought to life in the future, The Duskbloods sounded like the next best thing. Nintendo is likely banking on that, too, but the unfortunate truth is that the road to that kind of success isn't so simple.

The Duskbloods was originally expected to launch in 2026, but FromSoftware has delayed the project until next year. With Nintendo already having a massive end-of-year exclusive with the Ocarina of Time remake and GTA 6 gearing up to overshadow the next few months, delaying the game until 2027 is the right call.

Sharing a spooky Victorian-inspired world design and guns aren't enough to convince die-hard Bloodborne fans to give The Duskbloods a try. There are plenty of Bloodborne fans who don't own a Switch 2, and it would take a very special game to convince people to buy a brand-new system, especially in this never-ending era of rising console prices. If The Duskbloods really was a true spiritual successor to Bloodborne , it could probably convince a lot of people. However, the game's multiplayer focus quickly squashed many FromSoftware fans' initial excitement about the project.

Based on early hands-on previews, The Duskbloods gameplay is a smorgasbord of staple FromSoftware features thrust into a PvPvE world. FromSoftware has never shied away from experimenting with its own formula, but The Duskbloods could prove to be too far removed for many of the developer's longtime fans. Even if The Duskbloods can't capture the usual FromSoftware fan base, though, there is still a chance for Nintendo to have success with an exclusive that is this bold and risky.

Nintendo Doesn't Need Bloodborne Fans to Achieve Its Own FromSoftware Success Story

A scenario where The Duskbloods is to Nintendo what Bloodborne is to PlayStation feels unlikely right now, but nothing is impossible. Longtime FromSoftware loyalists might not migrate over to the world of Nintendo, but the Switch 2 already has plenty of users who are passionate about the company's exclusives, regardless of genre. The Duskbloods is incredibly different from the usual Nintendo staples like The Legend of Zelda , Super Mario , Metroid , and Donkey Kong . At first, that sounds like a disadvantage, but it can actually work wonders in The Duskbloods ' favor, because it brings something entirely new to table.

Bloodborne's Huge 2026 Sales Come With a Catch for The Duskbloods
Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Just Became Switch 2's Biggest Test
FromSoftware Game The Duskbloods Hit With Big Release Date Delay
2026's Biggest GTA 6 Rival Isn't Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake

There's also the added bonus of the recent Elden Ring Switch 2 port. I know that not every gamer sticks to just one console; I certainly don't. There is a lot of overlap, but there are also plenty of Nintendo fans who had probably never played a FromSoftware game until the Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition came to the console. This has given a lot of users a taste of what FromSoftware games are all about, and that could make The Duskbloods a hit that boasts years' worth of longevity for Nintendo. Either way, The Duskbloods will be the ultimate test of whether Nintendo and FromSoftware are a partnership that works or not.

item.title: New Switch 2 Roguelike Has a Twist That Could Give Hades Real Competition
item.description:
Roguelikes have a weird way of making failure entertaining, and Hades is probably one of the best examples of how well this approach works. Players can basically spend the entire run trying to defeat their enemies, fail miserably, but still start all over again and even be happy to do it because there is simply always another approach worth trying. It is a clever formula that encourages replayability aggressively, which is one of the reasons why Hades is such a recognizable name in the genre, after all. It seems like Tenjutsu is very aware of what made Hades so successful, and the game is trying to build upon this idea.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

In Tenjutsu , players' decisions don't just determine how the next encounter will play out but also how difficult future enemies become. The new title was developed by the designer of Dead Cells , and it is expected to launch on Nintendo Switch 2 in 2027. And even though competing with Hades is a pretty huge challenge, the unusual approach to player choice gives the new title an opportunity to bring something different to the genre.

Hades 2: All Romanceable Characters

The original Hades had such intriguing, unique romances. Hades 2 continues this tradition with its own twist on love for Melinoe.

By Juliet Childers

Tenjutsu Makes Every Strategic Decision Matter Far Beyond the Next Fight

Usually, roguelike action games give players several enemies to defeat, and it doesn't really matter which one they are going to kill first. In Tenjutsu , the city is controlled by four criminal syndicates, and although players can dismantle them in whatever order they want, the organizations they leave standing will become progressively stronger and more difficult to defeat. This creates an interesting dilemma, because if a player chooses an easier target to start with, the other ones that are more difficult anyway will become even more challenging. But then, if a player tackles the more difficult ones first, the easy ones will no longer be easy by the time it's their turn.

So, instead of just having players react to whatever pops up in front of them, the game actually requires them to think about what strategy would be the most beneficial. Moreover, getting rid of criminal syndicates comes with other benefits as well, because players get to gradually reclaim the city and rebuild it. This includes opening shops and restaurants, unlocking shortcuts, acquiring new weapons, and getting access to combat techniques. This gives the game a very solid progression system, and considering how important this is to the roguelike genre, having an entire city to restore is great by many people's standards.

If the developers manage to play their cards right, Tenjutsu could become a worthy opponent of Hades.

What makes this particularly appealing is that players will have something tangible to show for their progress, especially since an open shortcut, for example, can change the way subsequent runs are experienced. So, in other words, not every achievement is about making a player's character more powerful, and to be fair, transforming a place is always a rewarding experience. Of course, even the best idea in the world cannot save a game if fighting the enemies included feels repetitive and boring. This is particularly important for roguelikes because players are expected to fight a lot anyway, but fortunately, Tenjutsu 's combat is all about fast-paced encounters, martial arts, and different types of weapons, with an emphasis on tactical precision and experimentation.

Hades has already established its combat system, and many players seem to enjoy it, but putting martial arts at the center of the experience is what gives Tenjutsu an opportunity to distinguish itself. Moreover, by combining different weapons and fighting techniques, players will have another reason to experiment with the way they approach their enemies. In any case, whether the combat will be satisfying enough to compete with Hades still remains to be seen.

Tenjutsu Could Make Every Step of Progression a Double-Edged Sword

Going back to that interesting faction mechanic, it's important to note that eliminating a criminal syndicate doesn't just remove an enemy from the equation because it also contributes to rebuilding the city. In other words, spending more time developing the city means that other organizations still remain active and continue growing stronger. So, making progress in one area doesn't mean that the game becomes easier. However, maybe certain upgrades and shortcuts could be useful against specific syndicates, so paying attention to the city may turn out to be equally important anyway.

For example, players might deliberately leave a dangerous organization standing so they can work towards unlocking a specific area in the city that will give them a better chance to defeat their enemies later. In any case, Tenjutsu could actually make planning ahead an important part of mastering the game's mechanics, so even the most experienced players may have to think twice before committing to a strategy. Of course, there are plenty of hypothetical scenarios to develop here, but overall, if the devs manage to play their cards right, Tenjutsu could become a worthy opponent of Hades .

item.title: The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel Has a Huge Advantage Skyrim Never Had
item.description:
Bethesda finally gave The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel its official name on November 3, 2026, and the timing feels pretty fitting. Skyrim turns 15 on November 11, yet its successor still has no release date or gameplay reveal. The announcement also points toward Hammerfell, which is already an exciting change of scenery after Skyrim 's snowy mountains. For me, though, there's a far more interesting reason to be excited about what Bethesda does next, and it has very little to do with the teaser itself.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

When Skyrim launched in 2011, Bethesda had to make its own bets about what players would enjoy for years to come. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is in a completely different position, with the benefit of a modding community that has spent almost 15 years expanding Skyrim and finding ways around its limitations. Bethesda now has a remarkably detailed record of what players have wanted to change about its Elder Scrolls formula, along with countless examples of how those changes work in practice.

New Skyrim Mod Just Raised the Bar for The Elder Scrolls 6

A new Skyrim mod is bringing Hammerfell to life in impressive detail, raising expectations for whatever Bethesda ultimately does with The Elder Scroll

By Jane Vincent

Skyrim's Modding Community Has Spent 15 Years Showing Bethesda What Works

The scale of that work is hard to ignore. As of November 4, 2026, Nexus Mods lists more than 140,000 mods for Skyrim Special Edition alone. Some make tiny adjustments, while others rebuild entire systems or add enormous new areas. Every player has different preferences, of course, but the sheer amount of experimentation gives Bethesda an incredible resource to draw from. The studio can see which ideas creators keep returning to, which features have remained popular, and how far Skyrim 's original mechanics can be pushed. It's the kind of insight developers usually have to gather through years of feedback and playtesting, except Bethesda has an entire community doing it for free.

Todd Howard has already acknowledged some of Skyrim 's limitations. Speaking to IGN in 2021, he admitted that certain parts of the game lacked depth, particularly when it came to interactivity. That's exactly where the modding scene becomes so valuable. The modding community has spent years showing Bethesda how Skyrim 's systems can go further. Players have created their own solutions to problems with the original game, often transforming mechanics that Bethesda barely expanded on. And with official additions like Survival Mode and fishing eventually making their way into Skyrim , Bethesda has already demonstrated an interest in expanding the experience beyond its original design.

The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is in a completely different position, with the benefit of a modding community that has spent almost 15 years expanding Skyrim and finding ways around its limitations.

One of the clearest examples is Frostfall, which makes cold weather and exposure something players actually have to consider. Combined with the camping systems associated with Campfire, it turns a routine trip through the mountains into an expedition that takes planning. I wouldn't necessarily want every journey in Sentinel to become a survival exercise, but a world where its environment genuinely influences how I play sounds fantastic. Hammerfell's deserts are especially well suited to this kind of environmental interaction, giving Bethesda a chance to make travel and preparation feel more meaningful without simply copying Skyrim 's freezing wilderness.

There's a similar lesson in mods like Immersive Citizens, which adjusts how NPCs go about their lives and react to events around them. Skyrim can be wonderfully atmospheric, but its settlements sometimes feel like places that exist mainly for the player. More convincing routines and reactions would make Sentinel 's towns feel much more alive, especially if different settlements have their own customs and daily activities. Bethesda has an opportunity to make its world feel more believable through the small interactions that players encounter constantly, rather than relying entirely on major quests and scripted events.

Character Customization Could Go Much Further in Sentinel

Skyrim already gives players plenty of freedom, but its mods have exposed just how restrictive certain aspects of its character creation can feel. Alternate Start – Live Another Life is one of my favorite examples of this, because it lets players skip the familiar Helgen opening and begin their adventure with an entirely different background. That changes the tone of a playthrough before the main quest even begins. I'd love to see Sentinel embrace that kind of freedom, allowing players to establish their character's place in Hammerfell before becoming involved in whatever central conflict Bethesda has planned.

The same thinking applies to character progression. Ordinator – Perks of Skyrim completely overhauls the perk trees, opening up far more specialized builds than the original system supports. Then there's SkyUI, which demonstrates how much a better inventory interface can improve everyday gameplay. These mods address different frustrations, but both show how much room there is to refine Skyrim 's RPG systems. Bethesda doesn't need to make Sentinel overwhelmingly complicated to give players more control. Meaningful character builds and an interface that makes experimenting with them enjoyable would already be a significant improvement.

Sentinel Has a Chance to Learn Without Losing What Makes Elder Scrolls Special

Of course, Bethesda shouldn't treat every popular mod as something that belongs in Sentinel . Some players love demanding survival mechanics, while others just want to spend an evening exploring without worrying about hunger or exhaustion. Bethesda finally gave The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel its official name on November 3, 2026, and the timing feels pretty fitting. Skyrim turns 15 on November 11, yet its successor still has no release date or gameplay reveal. The announcement also points toward Hammerfell, which is already an exciting change of scenery after Skyrim 's snowy mountains. For me, though, there's a far more interesting reason to be excited about what Bethesda does next, and it has very little to do with the teaser itself.

When Skyrim launched in 2011, Bethesda had to make its own bets about what players would enjoy for years to come. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is in a completely different position, with the benefit of a modding community that has spent almost 15 years expanding Skyrim and finding ways around its limitations. Bethesda now has a remarkably detailed record of what players have wanted to change about its Elder Scrolls formula, along with countless examples of how those changes work in practice.

New Skyrim Mod Just Raised the Bar for The Elder Scrolls 6

A new Skyrim mod is bringing Hammerfell to life in impressive detail, raising expectations for whatever Bethesda ultimately does with The Elder Scroll

By Jane Vincent

Skyrim's Modding Community Has Spent 15 Years Showing Bethesda What Works

The scale of that work is hard to ignore. As of November 4, 2026, Nexus Mods lists more than 140,000 mods for Skyrim Special Edition alone. Some make tiny adjustments, while others rebuild entire systems or add enormous new areas. Every player has different preferences, of course, but the sheer amount of experimentation gives Bethesda an incredible resource to draw from. The studio can see which ideas creators keep returning to, which features have remained popular, and how far Skyrim 's original mechanics can be pushed. It's the kind of insight developers usually have to gather through years of feedback and playtesting, except Bethesda has an entire community doing it for free.

Todd Howard has already acknowledged some of Skyrim 's limitations. Speaking to IGN in 2021, he admitted that certain parts of the game lacked depth, particularly when it came to interactivity. That's exactly where the modding scene becomes so valuable. The modding community has spent years showing Bethesda how Skyrim 's systems can go further. Players have created their own solutions to problems with the original game, often transforming mechanics that Bethesda barely expanded on. And with official additions like Survival Mode and fishing eventually making their way into Skyrim , Bethesda has already demonstrated an interest in expanding the experience beyond its original design.

The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is in a completely different position, with the benefit of a modding community that has spent almost 15 years expanding Skyrim and finding ways around its limitations.

One of the clearest examples is Frostfall, which makes cold weather and exposure something players actually have to consider. Combined with the camping systems associated with Campfire, it turns a routine trip through the mountains into an expedition that takes planning. I wouldn't necessarily want every journey in Sentinel to become a survival exercise, but a world where its environment genuinely influences how I play sounds fantastic. Hammerfell's deserts are especially well suited to this kind of environmental interaction, giving Bethesda a chance to make travel and preparation feel more meaningful without simply copying Skyrim 's freezing wilderness.

There's a similar lesson in mods like Immersive Citizens, which adjusts how NPCs go about their lives and react to events around them. Skyrim can be wonderfully atmospheric, but its settlements sometimes feel like places that exist mainly for the player. More convincing routines and reactions would make Sentinel 's towns feel much more alive, especially if different settlements have their own customs and daily activities. Bethesda has an opportunity to make its world feel more believable through the small interactions that players encounter constantly, rather than relying entirely on major quests and scripted events.

Character Customization Could Go Much Further in Sentinel

Skyrim already gives players plenty of freedom, but its mods have exposed just how restrictive certain aspects of its character creation can feel. Alternate Start – Live Another Life is one of my favorite examples of this, because it lets players skip the familiar Helgen opening and begin their adventure with an entirely different background. That changes the tone of a playthrough before the main quest even begins. I'd love to see Sentinel embrace that kind of freedom, allowing players to establish their character's place in Hammerfell before becoming involved in whatever central conflict Bethesda has planned.

The same thinking applies to character progression. Ordinator – Perks of Skyrim completely overhauls the perk trees, opening up far more specialized builds than the original system supports. Then there's SkyUI, which demonstrates how much a better inventory interface can improve everyday gameplay. These mods address different frustrations, but both show how much room there is to refine Skyrim 's RPG systems. Bethesda doesn't need to make Sentinel overwhelmingly complicated to give players more control. Meaningful character builds and an interface that makes experimenting with them enjoyable would already be a significant improvement.

Of course, Bethesda shouldn't treat every popular mod as something that belongs in Sentinel . Some players love demanding survival mechanics, while others just want to spend an evening exploring without worrying about hunger or exhaustion.
